question: Tamar pays a £100m premium for Wychwood. Synergies phase in over two years — half the run rate in year one, the full amount from year two, forever — with a £20m one-off integration cost in year one. Tax is 25 % and Tamar discounts at 8 %. Roughly what annual pre-tax run rate of synergies does the deal need just to cover the premium?
model_answer_md:
About **£12.6m a year pre-tax**.

The machinery, for a run rate $S$: after tax the recurring saving is $0.75S$. Year one delivers half the run rate less the integration cost, all taxed: $(0.5S - 20) \times 0.75$, discounted one year. From year two the full after-tax amount runs as a perpetuity, $0.75S \div 0.08$, valued at the end of year one and discounted back.

Check £12.6m against the £100m hurdle:

- Year one: $(6.3 - 20) \times 0.75 = -£10.3\text{m}$, worth $-£9.5\text{m}$ today — the programme starts underwater.
- Perpetuity: $12.6 \times 0.75 = £9.45\text{m}$ a year; $9.45 \div 0.08 = £118.1\text{m}$ at end-year one; $118.1 \div 1.08 = £109.4\text{m}$ today.
- Total: $109.4 - 9.5 \approx £100\text{m}$. Covered, exactly.

Tamar's actual programme claims £20m — roughly £167m of value on the same arithmetic — so the deal clears its hurdle with room for the plan to disappoint by about a third.
key_points: Breakeven run rate ≈ £12.6m pre-tax against the £100m premium
Tax the synergies and the integration cost alike: everything at 75 %
Half-rate year one minus the one-off cost makes year one negative
Run rate ÷ discount rate as a perpetuity from year two, discounted back
Tamar's claimed £20m is worth ≈ £167m — comfortable cover

follow_ups.question: The integration takes twice as long — a four-year phase-in. What happens to the value?
follow_ups.answer_md: Every year of delay pushes full run-rate money further into the discount factor's teeth, so the value falls and the breakeven run rate rises. The one-off cost still lands early, so the early years get worse at both ends: less saving arriving, same money spent. Slippage in the phase-in is the quietest way a deal that cleared its premium on paper fails to in practice — the run rate is eventually achieved, just too late to be worth enough.

follow_ups.question: Why does the breakeven matter more than the headline synergy number?
follow_ups.answer_md: Because it converts the deal into a single falsifiable question: does management's number clear the hurdle, and by how much? Tamar claiming £20m against a £12.6m breakeven means the plan can fall a third short and still justify the premium. A deal whose claimed synergies sit *at* breakeven has no margin for the usual disappointments — and one below it is a transfer to the seller's shareholders, announced with a straight face.

weak_answer_note: Dividing the premium by the pre-tax run rate as if a pound of synergy were a pound of value — forgetting tax, the phase-in and the integration cost. That shortcut suggests £5m covers it; the honest arithmetic says £12.6m.
